```{r}
#| label: setup
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(knitr)
library(patchwork)
source(here::here("R", "wq_synthesis_helpers.R"))
source(here::here("R", "read_river_wq.R"))
source(here::here("R", "wq_target_metrics.R"))
source(here::here("R", "zone_release.R"))

store <- here::here("_targets")
tr <- function(x) targets::tar_read_raw(x, store = store)

chem    <- tr("lake_chem_2026")
lw      <- tr("wq_lake_long")
ann     <- tr("wq_annual")
trends  <- tr("wq_trends")
cps     <- tr("wq_changepoints")
tli     <- tr("lake_tli_annual")
ctd     <- tr("lake_ctd_2026")
ctdm    <- tr("ctd_cast_metrics")
kd      <- tr("ctd_par")
bpl     <- tr("buoy_profile_long")
be      <- tr("buoy_events")
bpd     <- tr("buoy_profile_daily")
me      <- tr("met_events")
mann    <- tr("met_annual_era5")
alum    <- tr("alum_al_daily")
alum26  <- tr("alum_dose_2026")
pcomp   <- tr("puarenga_compliance")
rwq     <- tr("river_wq_data")
rann    <- tr("river_wq_annual")
rtr     <- tr("river_wq_trends")
loads   <- tr("pc10_check_loads")
sl      <- tr("pc10_stream_loads")
pflow   <- tr("pc10_daily_flow")
dla     <- tr("driver_lake_annual")
dcor    <- tr("driver_lake_correlations")
airport <- tr("airport_met")
buoymet <- tr("all_buoy_met_data")
ctdth   <- tr("ctd_thermal")
buoyth  <- tr("buoy_thermal")
hflux   <- tr("hyp_flux")
hod     <- tr("hod_events")
hyps    <- tr("lake_hyps")
burger  <- read.csv(here::here("website", "data", "burger2007_chamber_fluxes.csv"))
enso    <- tr("enso_indices")
stab    <- tr("lake_stability")
sdrv    <- tr("strat_drivers")

theme_set(
  theme_bw(base_size = 11) +
    theme(
      panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "grey80", linewidth = 0.3),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
    )
)
pal_site <- c("Site 2" = "#0072B2", "Site 5" = "#D55E00", "Lake (mean of sites)" = "black")
pal_layer <- c(INT = "#009E73", HYP = "#E69F00", BOT = "#CC79A7")
var_lab <- c(tp = "TP (mg/m³)", tn = "TN (mg/m³)", drp = "DRP (mg/m³)", nh4 = "NH4-N (mg/m³)",
             nnn = "NOx-N (mg/m³)", chla = "Chl-a (mg/m³)", secchi = "Secchi (m)",
             pp = "TP − DRP (mg/m³)", org_n = "Organic N (mg/m³)", tn_tp = "TN:TP (molar)",
             turb = "Turbidity (NTU)")

# Daily Al dose (kg) runs to Feb 2026; the 2022-26 dosing workbook gives alum volumes (L/day) to Jul 2026.
# Extend kg Al to 30 Jun 2026 with each stream's median kg Al per L over the overlap (about 0.057; monthly range 0.04-0.06).
al_per_l <- alum |> inner_join(alum26, by = "date") |> mutate(m = format(date, "%Y-%m")) |>
  group_by(m) |> summarise(p = sum(puarenga_kg_al) / sum(puarenga_l_d), u = sum(utuhina_kg_al) / sum(utuhina_l_d)) |>
  summarise(p = median(p, na.rm = TRUE), u = median(u, na.rm = TRUE))
alum_est_from <- max(alum$date) + 1
alum <- bind_rows(alum |> mutate(estimated = FALSE),
                  alum26 |> filter(date >= alum_est_from, date <= as.Date("2026-06-30")) |>
                    transmute(date, utuhina_kg_al = utuhina_l_d * al_per_l$u, puarenga_kg_al = puarenga_l_d * al_per_l$p,
                              total_kg_al = utuhina_kg_al + puarenga_kg_al, estimated = TRUE))

# Alum dosing milestones
utu_start <- as.Date("2006-06-15"); pua_start <- as.Date("2010-01-14")
pua_pause <- run_events(alum$date, alum$date > as.Date("2012-01-01") & alum$puarenga_kg_al < 1,
                        min_len = 60, max_gap = 10)
pua_pause_main <- pua_pause |> slice_max(duration, n = 1)
alum_vlines <- function(hy = TRUE) {
  x <- if (hy) c(2006.5, 2010) else c(utu_start, pua_start)
  geom_vline(xintercept = x, linetype = 2, colour = "grey50", linewidth = 0.4)
}
fmt_trend <- function(pct, p) ifelse(is.na(pct), "–",
  paste0(ifelse(p < 0.05, ifelse(pct > 0, "▲ ", "▼ "), ""), sprintf("%+.1f", pct),
         ifelse(p < 0.05, "*", "")))
```

## Key findings {#sec-summary}

```{r}
#| label: summary-numbers
lake_tli <- tli |> filter(site == "Lake (mean of sites)")
tli_last <- lake_tli |> filter(hy == max(hy))
tli_min  <- lake_tli |> filter(hy >= 2010) |> slice_min(tli3_3yr, n = 1)
tli_max  <- lake_tli |> slice_max(tli3_3yr, n = 1)
mean_int <- function(v, hys) ann |> filter(layer == "INT", variable == v, hy %in% hys) |>
  summarise(m = mean(mean)) |> pull(m)
tp_0106 <- mean_int("tp", 2001:2006); tp_1220 <- mean_int("tp", 2012:2020)
tp_2122 <- mean_int("tp", 2021:2022); tp_2326 <- mean_int("tp", 2023:2026)
tn_0106 <- mean_int("tn", 2001:2006); tn_1220 <- mean_int("tn", 2012:2020); tn_2326 <- mean_int("tn", 2023:2026)
ch_0106 <- mean_int("chla", 2001:2006); ch_1220 <- mean_int("chla", 2012:2020); ch_2326 <- mean_int("chla", 2023:2026)
```

**The lake today.** Lake Rotorua is a eutrophic, polymictic lake.

- The 3-year mean TLI3 for 2024–2026 is **`r sprintf("%.2f", tli_last$tli3_3yr)`** (hydrological year `r tli_last$hy`).
  - This is above the target of 4.2.
  - It is well below the 2004–2006 peak of `r sprintf("%.2f", tli_max$tli3_3yr)`.
  - It is higher than the 2014–2020 low of `r sprintf("%.2f", tli_min$tli3_3yr)`.
- Integrated surface-water means for 2023–2026: TP ≈ `r round(tp_2326)` mg/m³, TN ≈ `r round(tn_2326)` mg/m³, chl-a ≈ `r round(ch_2326, 1)` mg/m³.

**Three phases in the record.**

1. **Early-2000s eutrophic peak.**
   - TP ≈ `r round(tp_0106)`, TN ≈ `r round(tn_0106)`, chl-a ≈ `r round(ch_0106)` mg/m³ (2001–2006).
   - Frequent bottom-water anoxia, with summer bottom NH₄ and DRP above 400 and 50 mg/m³.
2. **Alum-era recovery, 2007 to about 2012.**
   - TP fell by about half, to ≈ `r round(tp_1220)` mg/m³ (2012–2020).
   - TN fell to ≈ `r round(tn_1220)` mg/m³ and chl-a roughly halved.
   - The step changes in TP, DRP and particulate P are detected in 2007–2010. They follow Utuhina dosing (from June 2006) and Puarenga dosing (from January 2010).
3. **A partial reversal since about 2016.** Over the last 10 years TP, TN and chl-a show significant increasing trends at both sites, and Secchi depth is decreasing at Site 5. Two things stand out:
   - **The 2020–2022 TP excursion.** Mean TP was ≈ `r round(tp_2122)` mg/m³ in 2021–2022. Bottom TP reached 160 mg/m³ and DRP 110–120 mg/m³ in summer 2021/22. Three things coincided:
     - a near-complete pause in Puarenga dosing (`r paste(format(pua_pause_main$start, "%b %Y"), "to", format(pua_pause_main$end, "%b %Y"))`);
     - the strongest lake heatwave and the longest buoy-recorded stratification (at least 70 days, Nov 2021 – Jan 2022; @sec-strat2122);
     - two low-load years (external TP ≈ 28–29 t/y).

     TP returned to about 19 mg/m³ once dosing resumed and the very wet 2023 brought a well-mixed year.
   - **Nitrogen is rising.** TN rose from about 300 to about 360 mg/m³ after 2021. This follows the high-flow 2023 and 2024 hydrological years, when modelled external TN loads were 814 and 706 t/y against the target of 435 t/y. In-lake NH₄ and NOx are also higher than in the 2010s.

**Drivers.**

- **Alum** is the strongest single correlate of lake TP and TLI (ρ ≈ −0.8). It is confounded with the time trend, but the 2019–2021 dosing pause acts as a natural experiment that supports a causal link.
- **Internal loading.** Year-to-year changes in summer air temperature track bottom-water oxygen and NH₄ accumulation. Hot, calm summers produce long stratification, anoxia and internal P and N release: 2008/09, 2010/11, 2014/15, 2017/18, 2021/22 and 2023/24.
- **Internal release rates.** The bottom layer below the thermocline (typically 9–12 m deep in summer) is only about 5 m thick on average. During stratified periods:
  - it loses oxygen at about 1.5 g O₂/m²/d (the depletion rate rises about 5 % per °C);
  - it gains NH₄ at about 25–80 mg N/m²/d and DRP at about 2–5 mg P/m²/d (lower bounds).

  These rates suggest roughly 3–15 t of DRP and 30–230 t of NH₄-N are released each summer from the deep sediments alone (@sec-internal).
- **External loads.** Wet years raise external loads (2011–2013, 2017–2018, 2023–2024) but tend to flush and mix the lake, so they reduce peak bottom DRP.
- **Warming.** The bias-corrected ERA5 record warms by about 1 °C over 1977–2025. Air-heatwave days have increased from typically 5–20 per year before 2016 to mostly 25–55 per year since then.

**Data-quality caveats.** These affect the interpretation of trends.

- **Method changes.** TP, DRP and TN were analysed by three laboratories and several methods [@hamill2022]. TN switched from TKN + NNN to direct persulphate TN in November 2009 (about 50 mg/m³ lower), which coincides with the TN step down.
- **2010–2019 P method.** The BOPRC TP and DRP method used from August 2010 to September 2019 reads high, because silica and arsenic interference adds to the result.
- **TP correction.** BOPRC applied the lake workbook's TP correction (TP_corr = 0.9767 TP − 1.47 mg/m³) to July 2015 – September 2019 but not to August 2010 – June 2015, which left an artificial step of about 2 mg/m³ in mid-2015. This analysis applies it to the whole period, which lowers 2011–2014 TP by about 1.9 mg/m³.
- **Reporting resolution.** Zeros and negatives in 2015–2020 and finer decimals from 2021 mean the "increasing DRP" trend over the last 10 years is not reliable.
- **Streams.** A synchronous TP rise and fall (2011–2019) across all streams, including spring-fed ones, matches the period of the interfering method and is analytical rather than catchment-driven.
- See @sec-dq.

## Data {#sec-data}

```{r}
#| label: tbl-inventory
#| tbl-cap: "Datasets used. All are read through the targets pipeline (`_targets.R`, section 5b)."
rng <- function(d) paste(format(min(d, na.rm = TRUE), "%Y-%m"), "to", format(max(d, na.rm = TRUE), "%Y-%m"))
tibble::tribble(
  ~Dataset, ~Content, ~Period, ~Target,
  "BOPRC lake chemistry (S2 & S5, PC10 Jun-26)", "TP, TN, DRP, NH4, NOx, TKN, chl-a, Secchi, pH, turbidity; integrated (INT), hypolimnion (HYP), bottom (BOT)", rng(chem$date), "`lake_chem_2026`",
  "BOPRC CTD profiles (S2 & S5)", "Temperature, DO, chl fluorescence, PAR, conductivity, turbidity, 1 m bins, ~monthly", rng(ctd$date), "`lake_ctd_2026`",
  "Old buoy (2007–2022) and new LERNZmp profiler (2022–)", "Daily temperature and DO profiles, 0.5 m bins; new buoy also pH, chl, turbidity, SpC, ORP", rng(bpl$date), "`buoy_profile_long`, `buoy_profile_daily`",
  "Buoy met (old + new)", "Air temp, RH, wind, rain, SW radiation", rng(as.Date(buoymet$Date)), "`all_buoy_met_data`",
  "MetService Rotorua Aerodrome", "Hourly met", rng(as.Date(airport$date)), "`airport_met`",
  "ERA5, bias-corrected to buoy/airport", "Daily air temp, rain, wind, SW, RH (continuous)", rng(me$daily$date), "`era5_corrected_daily_baseline`",
  "Alum dosing (BOPRC)", "Daily kg Al, Utuhina and Puarenga", rng(alum$date), "`alum_al_daily`",
  "Alum dose rates + Puarenga compliance", "L/day by plant; paired up/downstream TP, DRP, Al, pH", paste(rng(alum26$date), "; compliance", rng(pcomp$date)), "`alum_dose_2026`, `puarenga_compliance`",
  "BOPRC river WQ (new)", "12 sites; TN, TKN, NOx, NH4, TP, DRP, TSS, DO, pH, temp, Al, discharge", rng(rwq$date), "`river_wq_data`",
  "PC10 2026 loads (McBride 2026)", "Modelled daily flow and AED concentrations per inflow, 12 scenario sets", "1959-07 to 2026-06", "`pc10_stream_loads`, `pc10_check_loads`",
  "ENSO indices (NOAA)", "Monthly ONI, SOI, IPO, SAM",
    rng(enso$date[enso$index == "ONI"]), "`enso_indices`"
) |> kable()
```

**Notes on the data.**

- **Hydrological years.** Lake summaries use July–June hydrological years, named by the year they end. For example, 2022 is July 2021 to June 2022, and its summer is December 2021 to February 2022.
- **INT samples** are depth-integrated over the epilimnion (0 m to roughly 6–14 m).
- **BOT samples** are taken about 1 m above the sediment, at 18–22 m.
- **Trend tests** are seasonal Mann–Kendall tests on monthly medians with Sen slopes. They are not corrected for serial correlation, so p-values are optimistic.
- **Change points** are binary segmentation of deseasonalised monthly anomalies, with a conservative penalty.

**Known caveats.**

- **Site codes.** The alkalinity file uses EL805168 for Site 5, against EL802148 here.
- **Ōhau outlet record.** It may contain a lab or method change, which is not yet confirmed (see the Ōhau page).
- **Buoy met.** Units changed on 2023-10-23 (fixed in the pipeline), and buoy RH drifts.
- **Puarenga river site.** The routine site (Puarenga at FRI, EK598179) is **upstream** of the alum plant, so it does not show the effect of dosing.
- **Utuhina river site.** The Utuhina at Lake Rd site is downstream of its plant.

## In-lake nutrient chemistry {#sec-nutrients}

### Long-term patterns

```{r}
#| label: fig-annual-int
#| fig-cap: "Annual (hydrological-year) means of integrated epilimnion samples at Sites 2 and 5. Dashed lines mark the start of Utuhina (June 2006) and Puarenga (January 2010) alum dosing. Years with fewer than 6 sampled months are omitted."
#| fig-height: 8
v <- c("tp", "drp", "pp", "tn", "nh4", "nnn", "org_n", "chla", "secchi")
ann |>
  filter(layer == "INT", variable %in% v) |>
  mutate(variable = factor(var_lab[variable], var_lab[v])) |>
  ggplot(aes(hy, mean, colour = site)) +
  alum_vlines() +
  geom_line() + geom_point(size = 1.2) +
  facet_wrap(~variable, scales = "free_y", ncol = 3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal_site) +
  labs(x = "Hydrological year", y = NULL, colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

**Phosphorus.**

- **Before alum (1990s–2006).** Integrated TP was mostly 30–48 mg/m³. A high 1993/94 (≈ 80 mg/m³) reflects very few samples in that year.
- **Fall with dosing.** TP fell from about 40 mg/m³ in 2006 to 11–20 mg/m³ from 2011/12 (after the 2010–2019 TP correction, @sec-dq).
- **Composition.** DRP dropped from 5–15 mg/m³ to mostly ≤ 2 mg/m³ in the surface water. Most of the remaining TP is particulate or organic (TP − DRP), which also halved, from about 30 to 15 mg/m³.
- **2021–2022.** TP was clearly elevated (27–33 mg/m³), with DRP rising to 4–8 mg/m³. It then fell back to 18–21 mg/m³ in 2023–2026.

**Nitrogen.**

- **Peak.** TN was highest in 2000–2007 (≈ 450–575 mg/m³ at Site 2).
- **Step down.** It stepped down around 2009/10 (change point Aug 2009 at Site 2, Feb 2008 at Site 5) to about 300 mg/m³ in 2011–2021. The drop is almost all organic N (TKN − NH₄), which follows the fall in phytoplankton biomass.
- **Since 2022.** TN has risen to 340–365 mg/m³.
- **Inorganic N** is more variable:
  - NH₄ peaks in years of strong internal loading.
  - NOx-N was close to detection before 2011 and much higher afterwards: years such as 2012–2013, 2017–2018 and 2023–2024 have annual means of 40–140 mg/m³.
  - The NOx step in 2011 appears at both lake sites and, in part, in several streams. It may be partly analytical (@sec-dq), but high NOx after winter mixing is a real feature of the lake.

**Chlorophyll-a and clarity.**

- **Chl-a** peaked in 2001–2007 (20–30 mg/m³ annual means) and fell to 8–13 mg/m³ after 2012.
- **Secchi** depth improved from about 2.5 to about 3 m.
- **Last decade.** Both have edged back towards poorer conditions: chl-a 12–16 mg/m³ and Secchi 2.4–2.5 m in 2026.

### Seasonal cycle and how it has changed

```{r}
#| label: fig-seasonal
#| fig-cap: "Monthly median of integrated samples (both sites) for three periods: pre-alum, first decade of dosing, and the last decade."
#| fig-height: 6
lw |>
  filter(layer == "INT", variable %in% c("tp", "drp", "tn", "nh4", "nnn", "chla")) |>
  mutate(era = cut(date, as.Date(c("1980-01-01", "2006-07-01", "2016-07-01", "2030-01-01")),
                   labels = c("1990–2006 (pre-alum)", "2006–2016", "2016–2026")),
         month = factor(month.abb[as.integer(format(date, "%m"))], month.abb[c(7:12, 1:6)]),
         variable = factor(var_lab[variable], var_lab[c("tp", "drp", "tn", "nh4", "nnn", "chla")])) |>
  group_by(era, month, variable) |>
  summarise(med = median(value), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(month, med, colour = era, group = era)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point(size = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~variable, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("grey40", "#56B4E9", "#D55E00")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Monthly median", colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5))
```

**The seasonal cycle.**

- **Late summer and autumn (Feb–May).** After stratification breaks down, nutrients released from the sediment are mixed into the surface water. TP, DRP and NH₄ peak at this time.
- **Winter and spring (Jul–Oct).** NOx-N peaks, as the NH₄ is nitrified and the lake stays mixed.

**How the cycle has changed.**

- **TP and DRP.** The late-summer and autumn TP peak (March–April) is about half of its pre-alum size (about 27 against 56 mg/m³), and similar to 2006–2016. The large autumn DRP peak of the pre-alum era (about 20 mg/m³ in March) has disappeared.
- **Ammonium.** The autumn NH₄ peak is now the largest of the three periods (median about 50 mg/m³ in April).
- **Nitrate.** The winter NOx peak (July–October, about 60–100 mg/m³) is much larger than before.
- **Nitrogen overall.** Together these suggest that N released from the sediment in summer is now mixed and nitrified in winter, rather than taken up by phytoplankton.
- **Chl-a.** It no longer shows the large summer–autumn maxima of the early 2000s, and in the last decade the seasonal range is only about 8–14 mg/m³.

### Trends

```{r}
#| label: tbl-trends
#| tbl-cap: "Seasonal Mann–Kendall trends of integrated (INT) samples, as Sen slope in % of the period median per year. ▲/▼ and * mark p < 0.05."
v <- c("tp", "drp", "pp", "tn", "nh4", "nnn", "org_n", "chla", "secchi", "tn_tp")
trends |>
  filter(layer == "INT", variable %in% v) |>
  mutate(cell = fmt_trend(pct_per_yr, p),
         variable = factor(var_lab[variable], var_lab[v]),
         period = factor(period, c("full", "pre_alum", "alum_era", "last_10y"),
                         c("1990–2026", "1990–2006", "2006–2026", "2016–2026"))) |>
  select(variable, site, period, cell) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = period, values_from = cell) |>
  arrange(variable, site) |>
  kable()
```

**What the trends show.**

- **Whole record.** TP, DRP, particulate P, TN, organic N and chl-a are all decreasing, and Secchi is increasing. This reflects the alum-era recovery.
- **Last decade (2016–2026).** The direction has reversed:
  - TP is increasing by about 2 %/yr at both sites.
  - TN is increasing by about 1.5–1.8 %/yr.
  - Chl-a is increasing by about 3–4 %/yr.
  - Secchi depth is decreasing at Site 5.
- **DRP over the last decade.** The significant DRP increase over 2016–2026 is driven by the many zero values reported in 2015–2019 (@sec-dq). It should not be read as a real increase.
- **TN:TP.** The ratio has risen from about 25 to about 40 (molar). P limitation has strengthened under alum dosing.

### Bottom waters and internal loading

```{r}
#| label: fig-bottom
#| fig-cap: "NH4-N, DRP and TP in integrated (INT), hypolimnion (HYP) and bottom (BOT) samples at Site 5 (Site 2 is similar). Bottom-water accumulation in stratified summers is the signature of internal loading."
#| fig-height: 7
lw |>
  filter(site == "Site 5", variable %in% c("nh4", "drp", "tp"), date >= as.Date("1999-07-01")) |>
  mutate(variable = factor(var_lab[variable], var_lab[c("tp", "drp", "nh4")]),
         layer = factor(layer, c("INT", "HYP", "BOT"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(date, value, colour = layer)) +
  alum_vlines(hy = FALSE) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.6, linewidth = 0.3) + geom_point(size = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~variable, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal_layer) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "2 years", date_labels = "%Y") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, colour = "Layer")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-bottom-max
#| tbl-cap: "Annual maximum bottom-water (BOT) concentrations (mg/m³), mean of the two sites. These are a proxy for the strength of summer internal loading."
ann |>
  filter(layer == "BOT", variable %in% c("tp", "drp", "nh4")) |>
  group_by(hy, variable) |> summarise(max = round(mean(max)), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = variable, values_from = max) |>
  select(hy, tp, drp, nh4) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Hydrological year", "TP", "DRP", "NH₄-N"))
```

**Internal loading remains active.**

- Years with strong bottom-water accumulation (two-site mean of the annual bottom maxima: DRP above 50 mg/m³ and NH₄ above 400 mg/m³) are 2004, 2010, 2015, 2022 and 2025. 2016, 2021 and 2024 are close to these thresholds.
- Years with little accumulation are 2007, 2012–2014, 2017–2019, 2023 and 2026.
- **Bottom-water trends:**
  - Bottom TP and DRP have declined over the whole record, but show no decline over the last decade.
  - Bottom NH₄ has increased over the alum era at both sites (+1.8 to +4.6 %/yr).
- So alum has suppressed the P released from the sediment, but it has not removed it, and N release continues.
- The seasonal timing, the thermal controls and estimates of the release rates are in @sec-internal.

### Trophic Level Index

```{r}
#| label: fig-tli
#| fig-cap: "Annual TLI3 (chl-a, TP, TN) by site, and the lake 3-year rolling mean against the Rotorua target of 4.2. The grey line is TLI4 (including Secchi) for comparison."
lake_tli <- tli |> filter(site == "Lake (mean of sites)")
ggplot() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 4.2, linetype = 2, colour = "darkgreen") +
  alum_vlines() +
  geom_point(data = tli |> filter(site != "Lake (mean of sites)"),
             aes(hy, tli3, colour = site), size = 1.5, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_line(data = lake_tli, aes(hy, tli3_3yr), colour = "black", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_line(data = lake_tli, aes(hy, tli4_3yr), colour = "grey50", linewidth = 0.6) +
  annotate("text", x = 1996, y = 4.17, label = "Target 4.2", colour = "darkgreen", hjust = 0, vjust = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal_site) +
  labs(x = "Hydrological year", y = "TLI", colour = NULL)
```

**The TLI trajectory.**

- **Peak.** The 3-year TLI3 peaked at 5.0 in 2004–2006.
- **Fall.** It fell steadily with dosing, and from 2013 to 2021 it stayed close to the target (4.10–4.25).
- **Recent years.** Since 2022 it has stayed at 4.3–4.4.
  - 2022 was the TP excursion year.
  - In 2024–2026 TN is higher and chl-a is creeping up.
  - 2026 has the highest annual chl-a (≈ 16 mg/m³) since 2009.

### Data quality and laboratory changes {#sec-dq}

The TP, DRP and TN records span several laboratories and analytical methods. This section sets out the method history from Appendix A of @hamill2022 and the metadata sheet of the BOPRC lake workbook [@boprc2026lakedata]. It then shows where the published TP correction has, and has not, been applied in the data used here.

#### Laboratory method history


```{r}

The top row shows the period the TP interference correction covers (dashed outline), the months already corrected in the supplied data (black) and the part left uncorrected (orange line). Bottom: integrated (INT) TP and TN at both sites as supplied, with method changes as vertical lines."
#| fig-height: 7.5
# lake_chem_2026 applies the "Metat data" TP correction consistently (correct_lake_tp() in R/read_river_wq.R):

tpc <- chem |>

  annotate("rect", xmin = as.Date("2010-08-20"), xmax = as.Date("2018-09-30"), ymin = 3.75, ymax = 4.25, fill = NA, colour = "black", linetype = 2) +

  annotate("rect", xmin = as.Date("2018-10-01"), xmax = as.Date("2019-06-30"), ymin = 1.6, ymax = 3.4, fill = "grey40", alpha = 0.25) +

p_ts <- lw |>
  filter(layer == "INT", variable %in% c("tp", "tn")) |>
  mutate(variable = factor(var_lab[variable], var_lab[c("tp", "tn")])) |>
  ggplot(aes(date, value, colour = site)) +
  geom_vline(data = chg, aes(xintercept = d), colour = "grey40", linetype = 3) +
  geom_point(size = 0.6, alpha = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~variable, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal_site) +
  scale_x_date(limits = as.Date(c("1990-01-01", "2026-07-01")), date_breaks = "2 years", date_labels = "%Y") +

```

**Phosphorus (TP and DRP).**

- **Before August 2008.** BOPRC analysed TP and DRP with the Murphy–Riley method. The listed detection limits were 8 (TP) and 4 (DRP) mg/m³, but values were recorded down to 1 mg/m³ [@hamill2022].
- **August 2008 to August 2010.** Samples went first to Hill Laboratories (detection limit 4 mg/m³), then from November 2009 to NIWA (1 mg/m³).
- **20 August 2010 to September 2019.** BOPRC brought the analysis back in-house on a flow-injection analyser. This method was later found to read high: silica and arsenic interfere with it, and the interference adds to the true value [@hamill2022]. The workbook notes that the interference was identified in February 2013 and the method was modified following Downes (1978) [@boprc2026lakedata].
- **October 2018 to September 2019.** BOPRC trialled a new method alongside the old one and adopted it in October 2019. In the paired trial samples the new method gave consistently lower TP and DRP [@hamill2022].
- **Correction factors.** @hamill2022tli derived correction factors for the lakes, applied to September 2010–September 2019. For the inflow streams the paired differences were too variable for a reliable correction, so @hamill2022 analysed streams before and after each method change separately. That report also argues that a falling stream TP or DRP trend across 2010 is reliable (the interference only adds), whereas a rising one needs support from the periods either side.

**Nitrogen (TN, TKN and NOx).**

- **To October 2009.** TN was calculated as TKN plus NNN (TN-K). The TKN detection limit was 90–100 mg/m³.
- **From November 2009.** TN is measured directly by alkaline persulphate digestion (TN-A). It is more precise but reads low when suspended solids are high (> 10 g/m³). @hamill2022 cites a comparison of lake means four years either side of the change that found TN-A about 50 mg/m³ lower. Other causes could not be ruled out.
- **Bearing on the step down in TN.** The TN step down identified above (change point August 2009 at Site 2) coincides with this method change. Part of the ≈ 150 mg/m³ fall in integrated TN may therefore be analytical, although most of it is organic N falling with chl-a.
- **Date discrepancy.** The workbook dates the switch from calculated TN to "2008" [@boprc2026lakedata]; @hamill2022 gives November 2009.
- **NOx before 2001.** NNN (nitrate + nitrite N) was analysed as nitrate-N only [@boprc2026lakedata].

#### The workbook metadata and the TP correction

The "Metat data" sheet of the lake workbook [@boprc2026lakedata] records the following.

**Data provenance.**

- Data from 1989 to July 2015 were transposed from the Lakewatch (Access) database to match the sites in Aquarius, which replaced Labstar in July 2015.

**Sampling.**

- Van Dorn discrete samples were used from 1989 to 2001. From 2001 the epilimnion has been sampled with an integrated tube (0–6 m), with discrete hypolimnion samples.
- `_HYP` samples are taken at hypolimnion depth (15 m at Site 2, 18 m at Site 5) whether or not the lake is stratified.
- `_BOT` samples are taken about 1 m above the bed.

**Other lab notes.**

- Chlorophyll-a: in-house spectrophotometric method (NIWA Stream Periphyton Monitoring Manual).
- Turbidity: APHA 2130 B (modified), white-light turbidimeter.
- The nutrient analysis moved to APHA 4500-P J (modified) by flow-injection analyser in October 2009.
- The sheet's own P-method table differs slightly from @tbl-lab-methods. It lists TP.1/DRP.1 for 2001–Sept 2008, TP.6/DRP.6 for Oct 2008–Oct 2009 at Hill Laboratories (DL 4), and TP.5/DRP.5 from Oct 2009, mostly at BOPRC with some NIWA.

**The TP correction.** The University of Waikato used duplicate P and ion analyses to derive a correction for the interference. It applies to the old BOPRC method:

$$
\mathrm{TP_{corr}} = -3.29420 + C + 0.976716\,\mathrm{TP_{old}}, \qquad C_\text{Rotorua} = 1.82649
$$

with TP in mg/m³. For Lake Rotorua this simplifies to $\mathrm{TP_{corr}} = 0.976716\,\mathrm{TP_{old}} - 1.468$.

- **When it applies.** The sheet specifies August 2010 to September 2018 inclusive, plus July–September 2019, which covers the gap between the end of the trial and adoption of the new method. Trial (October 2018–June 2019) and new-method (from October 2019) results are used unadjusted. The adjustment starts at the August 2010 step change, when analysis began at the BOPRC lab on 20 August 2010.
- **Size.** It removes 1.5 mg/m³ at 1 mg/m³ and 1.9 mg/m³ at 20 mg/m³ (≈ 10 % at typical integrated TP), and 2.4 mg/m³ at 40 mg/m³.
- **No DRP formula.** The sheet gives no correction for DRP.

```{r}
#| label: fig-tp-correction
#| fig-cap: "The TP correction in the supplied data and in this analysis. Left: each TP sample (all layers) from 2008 to 2021 as supplied, coloured by correction status; corrected values are identified because they back-transform exactly to whole mg/m³. Right: hydrological-year mean integrated TP (both sites) as supplied, and as used on this page and in the calibration targets, with the correction applied over the whole correction period."
#| fig-height: 4.5
pal_status <- c("Corrected in supplied data" = "#009E73", "In correction period, not corrected" = "#D55E00", "Outside correction period" = "grey55")
p_s <- tpc |>
  filter(date >= as.Date("2008-01-01"), date < as.Date("2021-07-01")) |>
  ggplot(aes(date, tp, colour = status)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.8, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_y_log10() + scale_colour_manual(values = pal_status) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "2 years", date_labels = "%Y") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "TP as supplied (mg/m³, log scale)", colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.direction = "vertical")
tpa <- tpc |>
  filter(layer == "INT") |>
  mutate(hy = wq_hy(date)) |>
  group_by(hy) |>
  summarise(`As supplied` = mean(tp), `Corrected consistently` = mean(tp_consistent), n_months = n_distinct(format(date, "%Y-%m")), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(n_months >= 6, hy >= 2005) |>
  pivot_longer(c(`As supplied`, `Corrected consistently`)) |>
  mutate(name = recode(name, `Corrected consistently` = "Corrected consistently (used here)"))
p_a <- ggplot(tpa, aes(hy, value, colour = name)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 2010.6, xmax = 2015.5, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = "#D55E00", alpha = 0.08) +
  geom_line() + geom_point(size = 1.2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`As supplied` = "black", `Corrected consistently (used here)` = "#0072B2")) +
  labs(x = "Hydrological year", y = "Mean integrated TP (mg/m³)", colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
p_s + p_a + plot_layout(widths = c(1.3, 1))
```

```{r}
#| label: tp-correction-numbers
cs <- tpc |> count(status)
gap <- tpc |> filter(status == "In correction period, not corrected")
gap_int <- gap |> filter(layer == "INT")
gap_range <- format(range(gap$date[gap$date < as.Date("2016-01-01")]), "%B %Y")
```

**How the supplied data stand.**

- **Corrected samples.** `r cs$n[cs$status == "Corrected in supplied data"]` TP samples in the supplied workbook are already corrected (all of July 2015–September 2018 except June 2016, plus July–September 2019). These are the non-integer TP values noted below. They are corrected values, not conversions from another unit.
- **Uncorrected samples.** `r nrow(gap)` samples inside the correction period are **not** corrected, almost all from `r gap_range[1]` to `r gap_range[2]`. This is the part of the record transposed from Lakewatch. The older "Lakes Data 1989_2025" workbook is the same.
- **Size of the gap.** Applying the correction to these samples lowers their integrated TP by `r sprintf("%.1f", mean(gap_int$tp - gap_int$tp_consistent))` mg/m³ on average (`r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * mean((gap_int$tp - gap_int$tp_consistent) / gap_int$tp))` %).
- **Effect if left as supplied.** The supplied record has an artificial TP step of about 2 mg/m³ between June and July 2015, and alum-era TP statistics mix corrected and uncorrected values.
- **What this analysis does.** The pipeline applies the correction to these samples (`correct_lake_tp()` in `R/read_river_wq.R`, used by `lake_chem_2026` and `chem_aeme`). Samples already corrected by BOPRC are recognised and left alone, and the value as supplied is kept in `tp_supplied`.
  - Every TP value on this page, and in the calibration targets, is the consistently corrected value.
  - The correction lowers annual mean integrated TP by about 1.8–1.9 mg/m³ in 2011–2014, and less in 2010 and 2015, which are only partly affected. The 3-year TLI3 over 2013–2021 is now 4.10–4.25.
- **DRP.** No correction is given or applied, so the interference remains in DRP for 2010–2019.

#### Reporting resolution

```{r}
#| label: fig-dq
#| fig-cap: "Reporting resolution of the integrated lake samples. Left: share of DRP values ≤ 1 mg/m³ and of zero or negative values. Right: share of TP values that are not whole numbers. Changes in either indicate method, detection-limit or laboratory changes."
#| fig-height: 4
dq <- lw |>
  filter(layer == "INT", variable %in% c("drp", "tp", "nh4", "nnn")) |>
  mutate(y = as.integer(format(date, "%Y"))) |>
  group_by(variable, y) |>
  summarise(low = mean(value <= 1), nonpos = mean(value <= 0),
            nonint = mean(abs(value - round(value)) > 1e-6), .groups = "drop")
p1 <- dq |> filter(variable == "drp") |>
  pivot_longer(c(low, nonpos)) |>
  ggplot(aes(y, value, fill = name)) + geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(low = "grey60", nonpos = "firebrick"),
                    labels = c(low = "≤ 1 mg/m³", nonpos = "≤ 0")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Share of DRP samples", fill = NULL, title = "DRP")
p2 <- dq |> filter(variable %in% c("tp", "drp", "nh4")) |>
  ggplot(aes(y, nonint, colour = variable)) + geom_line() + geom_point(size = 1) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Share non-integer", colour = NULL, title = "Reported precision")
p1 + p2
```

**Lake record.** The lake record has at least three visible reporting regimes:

1. **To about 2014.** Values are whole numbers in mg/m³, with detection limits of 0.5–1 mg/m³.
2. **2015–2020.** Many DRP values are reported as 0, with occasional −1 values in DRP, NOx and NH₄. TP is reported as non-integer values (e.g. 14.159744 and 16.113176). These are interference-corrected values: 16.113176 is the corrected value of a measured 18 mg/m³ (see the TP correction above).
3. **From 2021.** All nutrients are reported to 0.1 mg/m³.

**Effects on trends.**

- Trends in low-concentration surface DRP, NH₄ and NOx across these boundaries are unreliable.
- TP and TN trends are less affected, because concentrations are far above detection.

**River record.**

- TP at every stream, including the spring-fed Hamurana and Awahou streams, rises together from about 2011 and falls from about 2019 (@fig-river-anom).
- Spring-fed streams have stable, mainly geological P, so a shared step of about 20–30 % is much more likely to be analytical than a change in the catchment.
- River DRP is also high at most sites in 1993–1995 and 2003–2008, which may be a further reporting boundary.
- This matches the open question about a lab or method change in the Ōhau outlet record (labels change from "Labstar – Legacy" to "Routine" in July 2015, and grade codes change around 2020/21).
- @hamill2022 explains the river pattern. The 2010–2019 BOPRC P method suffered additive silica and arsenic interference, which varied more in the streams than in the lakes, so no reliable stream correction could be derived.
- **Recommendations:**
  - Ask BOPRC to apply the lake TP correction to August 2010 – June 2015 at source (this analysis already applies it).
  - Obtain the lake DRP correction from @hamill2022tli.
  - Analyse river TP and DRP within the method periods (before August 2010, August 2010 – September 2019, after October 2019) rather than across them.

## Buoy and CTD profiles {#sec-profiles}

### Temperature and oxygen structure

```{r}
#| label: fig-buoy-heatmap
#| fig-cap: "Weekly mean water temperature and dissolved oxygen from the old (2007–2022) and new (2022–2026) buoys, 1 m depth bins. The old buoy had thermistors at fixed depths and DO sensors only near the surface and bottom; the new profiler samples every 0.5 m. White areas are depths or periods without sensors."
#| fig-height: 7
hm <- bpl |>
  mutate(week = as.Date(cut(date, "week")), depth = round(depth_m)) |>
  group_by(week, depth) |>
  summarise(temp_c = mean(temp_c, na.rm = TRUE), do_mgl = mean(do_mgl, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(across(c(temp_c, do_mgl), \(x) ifelse(is.nan(x), NA, x)))
h1 <- ggplot(hm, aes(week, depth, fill = temp_c)) + geom_raster() +
  scale_y_reverse() + scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "C", na.value = "white") +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "2 years", date_labels = "%Y", expand = c(0, 0)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Depth (m)", fill = "Temp (°C)")
h2 <- ggplot(hm, aes(week, depth, fill = do_mgl)) + geom_raster() +
  scale_y_reverse() +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours = c("darkred", "orange", "lightyellow", "skyblue", "navy"),
                       values = scales::rescale(c(0, 2, 5, 9, 13)), limits = c(0, 14),
                       na.value = "white") +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "2 years", date_labels = "%Y", expand = c(0, 0)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Depth (m)", fill = "DO (g/m³)")
h1 / h2
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-strat-anoxia
#| fig-cap: "Share of buoy-monitored summer days (November–March) that were stratified (surface − bottom density difference > 0.2 kg/m³), hypoxic (bottom DO < 4 g/m³) or anoxic (bottom DO < 2 g/m³), by hydrological year. Numbers are the summer days with bottom DO data."
sm <- be$daily |>
  filter(as.integer(format(date, "%m")) %in% c(11, 12, 1, 2, 3)) |>
  mutate(hy = wq_hy(date)) |>
  group_by(hy) |>
  summarise(n = sum(!is.na(do_bot)),
            Stratified = mean(is_stratified(d_rho), na.rm = TRUE),
            Hypoxic = mean(do_bot < 4, na.rm = TRUE),
            Anoxic = mean(do_bot < 2, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(n >= 30)
sm |>
  pivot_longer(Stratified:Anoxic) |>
  mutate(name = factor(name, c("Stratified", "Hypoxic", "Anoxic"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(hy, value, fill = name)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  geom_text(data = sm, aes(hy, 1.03, label = n), inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 2.6) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#56B4E9", "#E69F00", "#D55E00")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Hydrological year", y = "Share of summer days", fill = NULL)
```

**Stratification is intermittent.**

- Rotorua stratifies for days to weeks at a time between November and March, and mixes in between.
- The longest buoy-recorded stratified periods are listed below:

| Summer | Longest stratified period |
|---|---|
| 2021/22 | ≥ 70 days (8 Nov 2021 – at least 16 Jan 2022)\* |
| 2014/15 | 52 days |
| 2008/09 | 51 days |
| 2010/11 | 46 days |
| 2019/20 | 42 days |
| 2017/18 | 41 days |
| 2023/24 | 38 days |

\* A minimum. The buoy's bottom temperature record stops on 16 January 2022, while the lake was still stratified, and resumes only on 21 February. The CTD casts show the lake mixed by 16 February (@sec-strat2122).

- Bottom anoxia (DO < 2 g/m³ for at least 3 days) builds within about 1–3 weeks of stratification setting in. The longest anoxic periods are listed below:

| Period | Duration of anoxia |
|---|---|
| Jan–Feb 2015 | 30 days |
| Jan–Feb 2009 | 28 days |
| Dec 2010 | 23 days |
| Feb 2010 | 21 days |
| Jan–Feb 2018 | 18 days |
| Jan 2024 | 18 days |

- **The record is uneven.** The 2022 gap between buoys and the sparser bottom DO in 2018–2022 mean that some events (e.g. summer 2021/22) are better captured by the CTD and bottom chemistry than by the buoy.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ctd-do
#| fig-cap: "Bottom (≥ 18 m) DO and surface–bottom temperature difference from the monthly CTD casts, 2003–2026. The dashed line marks 2 g/m³."
#| fig-height: 5
c1 <- ggplot(ctdm, aes(date, do_bot, colour = site)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 2, linetype = 2) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.5) + geom_point(size = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal_site) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Bottom DO (g/m³)", colour = NULL)
c2 <- ggplot(ctdm, aes(date, d_rho, colour = site)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = strat_drho_threshold(), linetype = 2) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.5) + geom_point(size = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal_site) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Δρ bottom − surface (kg/m³)", colour = NULL)
(c1 / c2) + plot_layout(guides = "collect") & theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

**CTD casts.**

- **Anoxia.** The casts confirm near-anoxic bottom water (minimum DO < 1 g/m³) in:
  - summer 2003/04 (Site 5), 2008/09 (Site 5) and 2009/10
  - summer 2015/16 (both sites at about 0.1 g/m³)
  - summer 2023/24 (Site 2, 0.7 g/m³)
- **Well-oxygenated summers.** 2011/12, 2020/21 and 2022/23 never fell below about 6 g/m³.
- **Strongest stratification.** ΔT reached 5.6–6.7 °C in summer 2017/18 and about 4 °C in 2014/15 and 2023/24.

### Light, chlorophyll and the new buoy sensors

```{r}
#| label: fig-light-chl
#| fig-cap: "Left: light attenuation Kd from CTD PAR profiles (r² > 0.8). Right: daily surface (≤ 2 m) chlorophyll fluorescence, pH, turbidity and specific conductance from the new buoy."
#| fig-height: 5
k1 <- kd |>
  ggplot(aes(Date, Kd)) + geom_point(size = 0.8, colour = "grey30") +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", span = 0.3, se = FALSE, colour = "#0072B2") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Kd (m⁻¹)")
k2 <- bpd |>
  filter(depth_m <= 2) |>
  group_by(date) |>
  summarise(`Chl fluor. (RFU)` = mean(chl_fl, na.rm = TRUE), pH = mean(ph, na.rm = TRUE),
            `Turbidity (NTU)` = mean(turb, na.rm = TRUE), `SpC (µS/cm)` = mean(spcond, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  pivot_longer(-date) |>
  ggplot(aes(date, value)) + geom_line(linewidth = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~name, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)
k1 + k2 + plot_layout(widths = c(1, 1.2))
```

**Light attenuation.** Kd from the CTD PAR profiles shifts in steps: about 0.35 m⁻¹ in 2003–2008, about 0.9 m⁻¹ in 2010–2016, back to about 0.35 m⁻¹ in 2020–2022, then rising again. Secchi depth improved over 2010–2016, when Kd suggests the water became darker, so these steps are more likely changes in the PAR sensor or in how the profiles were processed. Kd should not be used for trend analysis without checking the instrument history.

**New buoy, 2022–2026.**

- Surface chlorophyll fluorescence shows bloom episodes in late summer and autumn, and higher values in 2026.
- **Sensor caveats:**
  - **Conductance.** Specific conductance has a saw-tooth pattern of slow drift and abrupt steps, which matches sensor drift and recalibration at servicing rather than changes in the lake.
  - **Chlorophyll.** Fluorescence decays to a flat, low level through 2024–2025, which is typical of fouling.
  - **pH.** Surface pH drifted from about 7.5 (2022–2023) to about 6.7 (2025). This needs checking against discrete pH (see the pH page) before it is interpreted.
  - **CTD chlorophyll.** The CTD chlorophyll series also drops sharply in 2020–2021, at the same time as the drop in Kd, which suggests a sensor or calibration change rather than a real fall.
- The new-buoy data are most reliable for temperature and DO. They show bottom anoxia only in the summers of 2023/24 and 2024/25.

### Lake heatwaves

```{r}
#| label: tbl-lake-hw
#| tbl-cap: "Largest surface-water heatwaves from the buoy record (≥ 5 days above the day-of-year 90th percentile of 2007–2026). Intensity is relative to the day-of-year climatology."
be$heatwaves |>
  arrange(desc(max_anom)) |> head(12) |>
  transmute(Start = start, End = end, Days = duration, `Max temp (°C)` = round(max_temp, 1),
            `Max anomaly (°C)` = round(max_anom, 1), Category = category) |>
  kable()
```

**The strongest lake heatwaves.**

- December 2017 (20 days, +3.9 °C)
- Christmas 2021 to January 2022 (19 days, "strong")
- November 2025
- January 2024 and January 2015 (both coinciding with long anoxic periods)

The highest surface temperatures in the buoy record are 24–24.7 °C, in summer 2015/16, 2017/18, 2021/22 and 2023/24.

## Internal loading {#sec-internal}

Lake Rotorua is polymictic. It does not stratify through the whole summer like a deep monomictic lake. Instead it stratifies for days to weeks at a time between about October and March, and wind events mix it in between. Each stratified period isolates a thin bottom layer, roughly 3–8 m thick, over the deep sediments. That layer loses oxygen quickly and gains NH₄ and DRP released from the sediment. The next mixing event carries those nutrients into the surface water. This section uses the temperature profiles (buoys and CTD), the bottom-water chemistry and the lake hypsography to describe this cycle and to estimate the release rates.

### Seasonal cycle of stratification

```{r}
#| label: fig-thermal-season
#| fig-cap: "Seasonal cycle of thermal structure from the daily buoy profiles (2007–2026). Lines are the median by week of year and ribbons the 25–75th and 10–90th percentiles: surface–bottom temperature difference, Schmidt stability (from the lake hypsograph), thermocline depth (on stratified days only, density difference > 0.2 kg/m³, searched between 3 m and 2 m above the bed), and bottom (≥ 18 m) DO. Weeks are ordered July–June."
#| fig-height: 8
# Shallowest thermocline each buoy can resolve: the search starts at 3 m (thermocline_depth()) and readings are
# binned to 1 m, so the first interval is 3-4 m on the new buoy (0.5 m sensors) but 4-6 m on the old buoy
# (sensors 2 m apart from 0.5 m). A depth at that limit means "at or shallower than" it.
thermo_floor <- c(`new buoy` = 3.5, `old buoy` = 5)
bdaily <- buoyth |>
  mutate(at_floor = is.finite(thermo_depth) & thermo_depth <= thermo_floor[source] + 0.01) |>
  group_by(date) |>
  summarise(d_temp = mean(d_temp), d_rho = mean(d_rho), schmidt = mean(schmidt), thermo_depth = mean(thermo_depth, na.rm = TRUE),
            at_floor = any(at_floor), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(thermo_depth = ifelse(is.nan(thermo_depth), NA, thermo_depth)) |>
  left_join(be$daily |> select(date, do_bot), by = "date")
wk_order <- c(27:53, 1:26)
season_q <- bdaily |>
  mutate(wk = pmin(as.integer(format(date, "%U")) + 1, 53),
         wk = match(wk, wk_order)) |>
  pivot_longer(c(d_temp, schmidt, thermo_depth, do_bot)) |>
  filter(is.finite(value)) |>
  group_by(name, wk) |>
  summarise(q10 = quantile(value, .1), q25 = quantile(value, .25), q50 = median(value),
            q75 = quantile(value, .75), q90 = quantile(value, .9), n = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(n >= 10) |>
  mutate(name = factor(name, c("d_temp", "schmidt", "thermo_depth", "do_bot"),
                       c("ΔT surface − bottom (°C)", "Schmidt stability (J/m²)",
                         "Thermocline depth (m)", "Bottom DO (g/m³)")))
mlab <- tibble::tibble(wk = c(1, 5.4, 9.8, 14.1, 18.5, 22.8, 27.1, 31.5, 35.8, 40.2, 44.5, 48.9),
                       lab = month.abb[c(7:12, 1:6)])
ggplot(season_q, aes(wk)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = q10, ymax = q90), fill = "#0072B2", alpha = 0.15) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = q25, ymax = q75), fill = "#0072B2", alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_line(aes(y = q50), colour = "#0072B2") +
  geom_hline(data = tibble::tibble(name = factor("Bottom DO (g/m³)", levels(season_q$name)), y = 2),
             aes(yintercept = y), linetype = 2, colour = "firebrick") +
  facet_wrap(~name, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = mlab$wk, labels = mlab$lab) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-thermal-month
#| tbl-cap: "Monthly summary of thermal structure from the buoys (daily) and CTD casts (monthly, Sites 2 and 5): share of days or casts stratified (surface − bottom density difference > 0.2 kg/m³), median thermocline depth on stratified days, and median Schmidt stability."
mon <- function(d) d |> mutate(m = factor(month.abb[as.integer(format(date, "%m"))], month.abb[c(7:12, 1:6)])) |>
  group_by(m) |>
  summarise(strat = mean(is_stratified(d_rho)), zth = median(thermo_depth[is_stratified(d_rho)], na.rm = TRUE),
            ss = median(schmidt), .groups = "drop")
left_join(mon(bdaily), mon(ctdth), by = "m", suffix = c("_buoy", "_ctd")) |>
  transmute(Month = m, `Stratified (buoy)` = scales::percent(strat_buoy, 1),
            `Thermocline, m (buoy)` = round(zth_buoy, 1), `Schmidt, J/m² (buoy)` = round(ss_buoy, 1),
            `Stratified (CTD)` = scales::percent(strat_ctd, 1),
            `Thermocline, m (CTD)` = round(zth_ctd, 1)) |>
  kable()
```

**When the lake stratifies.**

- Stratification starts to develop in October and November.
- It is most frequent and strongest from December to February. About half of all summer days are stratified (in December–February the surface is then typically 1 °C or more warmer than the bottom), and Schmidt stability on calm, hot days exceeds 100–300 J/m².
- It collapses in March as the lake cools. From April to August the lake is fully mixed.
- **Thermocline depth.** On stratified days the thermocline is typically 9–12 m deep (monthly medians; interquartile range about 7–13 m). The isolated bottom layer therefore covers roughly a third to half of the lake bed, because the hypsograph is steep below 10 m.
- **The bottom layer is thin.** Its mean thickness (hypolimnion volume divided by its sediment area) is only about 4–6 m. A thin layer over a large sediment area is why oxygen falls so fast: below 2 g/m³ within 1–3 weeks of the onset of stratification.

### Stratified periods and the thermocline, summer by summer

```{r}
#| label: fig-thermo-summers
#| fig-cap: "Daily thermocline depth from the buoys (points, only on stratified days), coloured by bottom DO, for each summer (November–March). Lines join consecutive days with a thermocline. Open triangles are days when the thermocline was at the shallowest depth the buoy can resolve (5 m on the old buoy, whose sensors are 2 m apart, and 3.5 m on the new buoy), so the true depth was at or above it. Grey shading marks days with bottom DO < 2 g/m³. Gaps are periods without a thermocline (mixed) or without data."
#| fig-height: 10
sdat <- bdaily |>
  filter(as.integer(format(date, "%m")) %in% c(11, 12, 1, 2, 3)) |>
  mutate(summer = paste0(wq_hy(date) - 1, "/", substr(wq_hy(date), 3, 4)),
         doy = as.numeric(date - as.Date(paste0(wq_hy(date) - 1, "-11-01"))))
spath <- sdat |> filter(is.finite(thermo_depth)) |> arrange(date) |>
  mutate(run = cumsum(c(1, diff(as.numeric(date)) != 1)))   # a new run after any day without a thermocline
ggplot(sdat, aes(doy)) +
  geom_rect(data = \(d) filter(d, do_bot < 2), aes(xmin = doy - 0.5, xmax = doy + 0.5, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf),
            fill = "grey80") +
  geom_path(data = spath, aes(y = thermo_depth, group = run), colour = "grey40", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_point(data = \(d) filter(d, !at_floor), aes(y = thermo_depth, colour = do_bot), size = 0.7) +
  geom_point(data = \(d) filter(d, at_floor), aes(y = thermo_depth, colour = do_bot), size = 1.1, shape = 2) +
  scale_y_reverse(limits = c(20, 0)) +
  scale_colour_gradientn(colours = c("darkred", "orange", "gold", "skyblue", "navy"),
                         values = scales::rescale(c(0, 2, 4, 7, 11)), limits = c(0, 11),
                         na.value = "grey50") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 30, 61, 92, 120), labels = c("Nov", "Dec", "Jan", "Feb", "Mar")) +
  facet_wrap(~summer, ncol = 4) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Thermocline depth (m)", colour = "Bottom DO\n(g/m³)")
```

**Summer by summer.** The summers differ mainly in how long the stratified periods last and how often wind breaks them up.

- **Long stratified periods with prolonged bottom anoxia:** 2007/08, 2008/09, 2014/15, 2015/16, 2017/18 and 2023/24. In these summers the thermocline deepens steadily, by about 1 m a week, from 6–9 m to 12–16 m as the period goes on.
- **Long stratification without bottom-DO data:** 2019/20 and 2021/22 (grey points). The bottom chemistry shows strong accumulation in both. In 2021/22, the CTD casts show bottom anoxia in December (@sec-strat2122).
- **Short stratified periods separated by frequent mixing, with little anoxia:** 2011/12, 2012/13, 2013/14, 2016/17, 2022/23 and 2025/26.
- **Missing:** the 2009/10 and 2010/11 summers are largely missing from the buoy record.
- **Shallow thermoclines are censored.** The thermocline is searched for only below 3 m, so that near-surface daytime warming is not mistaken for it. With the old buoy's 2 m sensor spacing, the shallowest depth it can return is 5 m. About 15% of the old buoy's thermocline days (101 of 692) sit exactly at 5 m, mostly at the onset of stratification; for these the true thermocline was at 5 m or shallower. The new buoy (0.5 m spacing) can resolve thermoclines from 3.5 m, and only 12 of its 210 days sit at that limit. Monthly medians are barely affected, because most stratified days have deeper thermoclines.
- **New profiler (from 2022).** Thermocline depths are similar to the old buoy's: a median of about 10 m in November–December and about 13 m in January.

### What starts and ends stratification {#sec-strat-drivers}

Stratification is a balance between heating, which makes the surface water lighter and builds stability, and mixing. Mixing comes from wind stirring, and from surface cooling, which makes the surface water denser so that it sinks. This section uses only the buoy profiles and the lake meteorology to ask which of these sets up and which ends each stratified period.

- **Wind and air temperature** are the buoy's, with ERA5-BC filling the gaps (3% of stratified days for wind).
  - The buoy wind is already at 10 m: it was converted from the anemometer height with `metscale::wind_at_height()` when it was loaded.
  - ERA5-BC wind was bias-corrected to that 10 m wind, so it needs no further scaling.
- **Humidity** is ERA5. The old buoy's humidity reads 5–9% low and the new buoy's drifts from 2024, which would overstate evaporation. ERA5 agrees with the 2022–23 buoy and airport humidity to within 2–3%.
- **Radiation** (shortwave and longwave) is from ERA5-BC.
- **Daily stability** from the buoy profiles and the hypsograph (`rLakeAnalyzer`):
  - **Schmidt stability:** the energy needed to mix the lake fully.
  - **Lake number:** stability against wind stirring of the bottom water. Small values mean wind can mix it.
  - **Wedderburn number:** the same for the thermocline tilting up at the upwind end.
- **Surface heat budget:** bulk formulas from daily means, checked against the lake's measured change in heat content (from the buoy profiles and the hypsograph) over 168 well-covered months.
  - The surface fluxes lose about 17 W/m² more than the lake actually loses. The gap is largest in winter (27–36 W/m², May–August) and close to zero in summer (2–4 W/m², November–January).
  - The most likely cause is the ERA5 incoming longwave, which is not bias-corrected. It averages 323 W/m², against about 370 W/m² from an empirical clear-sky and cloud formula (Brutsaert with the ERA5 cloud cover). An underestimate that grows with cloud cover would match the winter pattern. The model calibration's longwave factor (0.9–1.2) points the same way.
  - Smaller contributions are possible from the difference between the 0.5 m water temperature and the skin temperature, from geothermal and spring inputs that are warmer than the lake in winter, and from the bulk transfer coefficients.
  - The heat budget is therefore used only as departures from the seasonal norm and as percentiles, which this bias does not affect.
- Code in `R/strat_drivers.R`; targets `lake_met_daily_tbl`, `lake_stability`, `strat_drivers` and `strat_event_1415`.

```{r}
#| label: sdrv-data
sd_daily <- sdrv$daily
sd_ev <- sdrv$events
sd_br <- sd_ev |> filter(type == "breakdown")
sd_on <- sd_ev |> filter(type == "onset")
# step 1: probability that a stratified day is followed by a mixed day, by Lake number
ln_next <- sd_daily |> arrange(date) |>
  mutate(next_mixed = !is_stratified(lead(d_rho))) |>
  filter(is_stratified(d_rho), is.finite(next_mixed), is.finite(lake_number))
ln_tab <- ln_next |>
  mutate(bin = cut(lake_number, c(0, 0.03, 0.06, 0.1, 0.2, 0.4, Inf),
                   labels = c("< 0.03", "0.03–0.06", "0.06–0.1", "0.1–0.2", "0.2–0.4", "> 0.4"))) |>
  group_by(bin) |> summarise(n = n(), p = mean(next_mixed), .groups = "drop")
p_lo_ln <- mean(ln_next$next_mixed[ln_next$lake_number < 0.1])
p_hi_ln <- mean(ln_next$next_mixed[ln_next$lake_number >= 0.1])
# step 3: baseline shares of the forcing classes on all stratified days
strat_days <- sd_daily |> filter(is_stratified(d_rho), is.finite(p_wind_pct), is.finite(q_net_pct))
cls <- function(w, q) case_when(w >= 0.75 & q <= 0.25 ~ "wind + cooling", w >= 0.75 ~ "wind",
                                q <= 0.25 ~ "cooling", TRUE ~ "neither")
cls_lev <- c("wind + cooling", "wind", "cooling", "neither")
cls_tab <- full_join(
  sd_br |> filter(!is.na(class)) |> count(class, name = "n_break"),
  strat_days |> mutate(class = cls(p_wind_pct, q_net_pct)) |> count(class, name = "n_days"), by = "class") |>
  mutate(across(starts_with("n_"), \(x) coalesce(x, 0L)),
         `Share of breakdowns` = n_break / sum(n_break), `Share of all stratified days` = n_days / sum(n_days),
         class = factor(class, cls_lev)) |>
  arrange(class)
pal_cls <- c("wind + cooling" = "#7B3294", wind = "#0571B0", cooling = "#E66101", neither = "grey55")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-strat-ln
#| fig-cap: "Step 1: daily stability numbers and the next day. Left: the share of stratified buoy days that were followed by a mixed day (density difference ≤ 0.2 kg/m³), by the Lake number on the stratified day; numbers are the days in each bin. Right: the Lake number and Schmidt stability on stratified days that stayed stratified and on those followed by mixing (log scales)."
#| fig-height: 4
g1 <- ggplot(ln_tab, aes(bin, p)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2166AC", width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0("n = ", n)), vjust = -0.4, size = 3) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))) +
  labs(x = "Lake number on the stratified day", y = "Mixed the next day")
g2 <- ln_next |>
  mutate(next_day = ifelse(next_mixed, "Mixed next day", "Stayed stratified")) |>
  select(next_day, `Lake number` = lake_number, `Schmidt stability (J/m²)` = st) |>
  pivot_longer(-next_day) |>
  filter(is.finite(value), value > 0) |>
  ggplot(aes(next_day, value, fill = next_day)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.size = 0.6, width = 0.6) +
  scale_y_log10() + facet_wrap(~name, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Mixed next day" = "#B2182B", "Stayed stratified" = "#92C5DE"), guide = "none") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)
g1 + g2 + plot_layout(widths = c(1, 1.3))
```

**Step 1: the stability numbers.**

- **The Lake number separates the days that hold from the days that break.**
  - On stratified days with a Lake number of 0.1 or more, the lake was mixed the next day `r scales::percent(p_hi_ln, 1)` of the time.
  - Below 0.1 it was `r scales::percent(p_lo_ln, 1)`, and above 0.4 it never happened (@fig-strat-ln).
- **Days that broke the next day already had low stability.** Their median Schmidt stability was about a third of that on days that held.
- **The threshold is low.** The textbook threshold for wind mixing (a Lake number of 1) is too high for Rotorua.
  - The lake is shallow and exposed and its stratification is weak, so the useful threshold is about 0.1.
  - Lake numbers from daily wind are also higher than in the windiest hours, which do the mixing.
- **The Wedderburn number behaves the same way.**
- **For the model:** a simulated lake that holds stratification for days at Lake numbers well below 0.1, or breaks at values above about 0.4, is mixing too little or too much.

```{r}
#| label: fig-strat-composite
#| fig-cap: "Step 2: composites of the days around the start (onset, left) and end (breakdown, right) of the buoy-recorded stratified periods; day 0 is the first stratified day or the first mixed day. Lines: mean over events; ribbons: 95% confidence interval of the mean. Wind (10 m), air − water temperature and net surface heat flux are departures from the seasonal norm (the mean for the same time of year, ±15 days, 2007–2026); positive heat flux means heating. Schmidt stability is the measured value."
#| fig-height: 7
comp_sum <- sdrv$composite |>
  select(type, lag, `Wind (m/s)` = wind_anom, `Air − water (°C)` = ta_tw_anom,
         `Heat flux (W/m²)` = q_net_anom, `Schmidt (J/m²)` = st) |>
  pivot_longer(-c(type, lag)) |>
  group_by(type, lag, name) |>
  summarise(m = mean(value, na.rm = TRUE), se = sd(value, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(sum(is.finite(value))), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(type = factor(type, c("onset", "breakdown"), c(sprintf("Onset (n = %d)", nrow(sd_on)), sprintf("Breakdown (n = %d)", nrow(sd_br)))),
         name = factor(name, c("Wind (m/s)", "Air − water (°C)", "Heat flux (W/m²)", "Schmidt (J/m²)")))
ggplot(comp_sum, aes(lag, m)) +
  geom_hline(data = \(d) filter(d, !grepl("Schmidt", name)), aes(yintercept = 0), colour = "grey50") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 2, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = m - 1.96 * se, ymax = m + 1.96 * se), fill = "#4393C3", alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_line(colour = "#08306B") + geom_point(size = 0.8, colour = "#08306B") +
  facet_grid(name ~ type, scales = "free_y", switch = "y") +
  labs(x = "Days from onset / breakdown", y = NULL) +
  theme(strip.placement = "outside", strip.text.y.left = element_text(angle = 90))
```

```{r}
#| label: sdrv-numbers
cs <- function(tp, var, lags) mean(sdrv$composite[[var]][sdrv$composite$type == tp & sdrv$composite$lag %in% lags], na.rm = TRUE)
on_w <- cs("onset", "wind_anom", -1:0); on_q <- cs("onset", "q_net_anom", -1:0); on_t <- cs("onset", "ta_tw_anom", -1:0)
br_w <- cs("breakdown", "wind_anom", 0); br_q <- cs("breakdown", "q_net_anom", 0); br_t <- cs("breakdown", "ta_tw_anom", 0)
st_pre <- cs("breakdown", "st", -7); st_last <- cs("breakdown", "st", -1)
```

**Step 2: the lead-up to onset and breakdown** (@fig-strat-composite; `r nrow(sd_on)` onsets and `r nrow(sd_br)` breakdowns with mixed days observed on the other side, 2007–2026).

- **Onset is calm and warm.**
  - On the day before and the day of onset, wind was `r sprintf("%.1f", -on_w)` m/s below normal and the net heat flux `r round(on_q)` W/m² above normal. The air was `r sprintf("%.1f", on_t)` °C warmer relative to the water than usual.
  - The calm spell builds over 1–2 days. A windy, cool spell often comes about a week before, so onsets typically follow the clearance of a front.
  - Schmidt stability doubles within a day of onset.
- **Breakdown is windy and cool.**
  - On the day of breakdown, wind was `r sprintf("%.1f", br_w)` m/s above normal and the heat flux `r round(-br_q)` W/m² below normal. The air was `r sprintf("%.1f", -br_t)` °C cooler relative to the water than usual: the signature of a cool change.
  - The wind and cooling are concentrated in days −1 to +1, so most breakdowns are sudden, not gradual.
- **The stability was already running down.** Schmidt stability fell from about `r round(st_pre)` J/m² a week before breakdown to `r round(st_last)` J/m² on the last stratified day. Over that week, heat input was lower than normal and the air cooled relative to the water. A weakened stratification was then finished by a windy or cool day.

```{r}
#| label: fig-strat-class
#| fig-cap: "Step 3: forcing at each breakdown, as day-of-year percentiles of the 3-day mean (days −2 to 0) of the wind energy flux (ρ Cd U10³) and the net surface heat flux, among all 3-day means at the same time of year (±15 days, 2007–2026). Dashed lines mark the class boundaries (wind ≥ 75th percentile; cooling ≤ 25th percentile). Point size is the peak Schmidt stability of the stratified period that ended. Grey points in the background are all other stratified days, for comparison."
#| fig-height: 5.5
ggplot(sd_br |> filter(!is.na(class)), aes(wind_pct, cool_pct)) +
  geom_point(data = strat_days, aes(p_wind_pct, q_net_pct), colour = "grey85", size = 0.6, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.75, linetype = 2) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0.25, linetype = 2) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = factor(class, cls_lev), size = st_peak), alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal_cls) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 6, name = "Peak Schmidt\nstability (J/m²)") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Wind energy flux, percentile (windier →)", y = "Net heat flux, percentile (← more cooling)", colour = "Breakdown class")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-strat-class
#| tbl-cap: "Step 3: breakdowns by forcing class, against the share of all stratified buoy days in each class (the share expected if breakdowns were unrelated to the weather). Medians per class: duration of the stratified period that ended, its peak Schmidt stability, and the maximum daily-mean 10 m wind over days −2 to 0."
cls_med <- sd_br |> filter(!is.na(class)) |> group_by(class) |>
  summarise(dur = median(duration), stp = median(st_peak, na.rm = TRUE), wmax = median(wind_max, na.rm = TRUE),
            early = mean(as.integer(format(day0, "%m")) %in% c(9, 10, 11)), .groups = "drop")
cls_tab |>
  left_join(cls_med, by = "class") |>
  transmute(Class = class, Breakdowns = n_break, `Share of breakdowns` = scales::percent(`Share of breakdowns`, 1),
            `Share of all stratified days` = scales::percent(`Share of all stratified days`, 1),
            `Duration (days)` = dur, `Peak Schmidt (J/m²)` = round(stp), `Max wind (m/s)` = round(wmax, 1),
            `Sep–Nov` = scales::percent(early, 1)) |>
  kable()
```

```{r}
#| label: sdrv-class-numbers
sh <- function(k, col = "Share of breakdowns") cls_tab[[col]][cls_tab$class == k]
forced <- 1 - sh("neither"); forced_base <- 1 - sh("neither", "Share of all stratified days")
```

**Step 3: what ended each stratified period** (@fig-strat-class, @tbl-strat-class).

- **Most breakdowns came with unusual weather.**
  - `r scales::percent(forced, 1)` of breakdowns had a top-quartile wind, a bottom-quartile heat flux or both over the three days up to breakdown. Only `r scales::percent(forced_base, 1)` of all stratified days had such forcing.
- **Wind and cooling together** is the most common forcing: `r scales::percent(sh("wind + cooling"), 1)` of breakdowns, against `r scales::percent(sh("wind + cooling", "Share of all stratified days"), 1)` of stratified days.
  - These are the cool, windy changes behind a front, and they end the longest and strongest stratified periods (median peak Schmidt stability about 85 J/m²).
  - Wind alone rarely does it (`r scales::percent(sh("wind"), 1)`). When it does, the period is usually shorter and weaker.
- **Cooling without strong wind** (`r scales::percent(sh("cooling"), 1)`) ends periods of ordinary strength, mostly in mid-summer, after several cool, cloudy days without unusually strong wind. The lake loses heat from the top until the surface layer is as dense as the water below.
- **No unusual forcing** (`r scales::percent(sh("neither"), 1)`): these are mostly mid-summer periods of modest strength, worn down by ordinary wind and night-time cooling.
  - Their forcing sits near the median, so Rotorua's summer stratification is often marginal and needs no event to end it.
  - The daily-mean budget also misses short events: an afternoon squall or one cold night can mix the lake without changing the daily mean much.
- **Reading.** Stratification is set up by calm, warm spells of one to two days and ended mostly by cool, windy changes. The long, anoxic stratified periods (@sec-strat2122 and @fig-thermo-summers) are those where calm, warm weather persisted and no strong front arrived for weeks.

#### A closer look: summer 2014/15 at hourly resolution {#sec-strat-1415}

The daily analysis can miss what happens within a day. This checks one stratified period against the old buoy's 15-minute record, averaged to hourly. The period is 19 December 2014 – 8 February 2015: the strongest stratification on record (peak Schmidt stability about 210 J/m²) and the 30-day bottom anoxia of early 2015.

```{r}
#| label: fig-strat-1415
#| fig-cap: "Summer 2014/15 from the old buoy's 15-minute record (hourly means). (a) Water temperature by depth (sensors at 0.5, 2.5, 4.5, 6.5, 8.5 m and 2 m apart below). (b) Bottom − surface density difference; dotted line at the 0.2 kg/m³ stratification threshold. (c) DO at 1 m and 20 m. (d) Wind at 10 m, with the daily mean (black). (e) Hourly net surface heat flux (grey) and its daily mean (black); positive is heating. Grey band: the stratified period in the daily record; dashed line: the hourly breakdown on 6 February."
#| fig-height: 10
ev <- tr("strat_event_1415")
eh <- ev$hourly
e_br <- as.POSIXct("2015-02-06", tz = "Etc/GMT-12")
e_band <- annotate("rect", xmin = as.POSIXct("2014-12-19", tz = "Etc/GMT-12"), xmax = as.POSIXct("2015-02-09", tz = "Etc/GMT-12"),
                   ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = "grey80", alpha = 0.35)
e_v <- geom_vline(xintercept = e_br, linetype = 2, colour = "firebrick")
e_x <- scale_x_datetime(date_breaks = "2 weeks", date_labels = "%d %b", expand = c(0, 0))
e_day <- eh |> mutate(day = lubridate::floor_date(hour, "day") + 12 * 3600) |> group_by(day) |>
  summarise(wind = mean(wind, na.rm = TRUE), q_net = mean(q_net, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
e_tmp <- ev$temp |> arrange(hour, depth) |> group_by(hour) |>
  mutate(top = (depth + lag(depth, default = 0)) / 2, bot = (depth + lead(depth, default = max(depth) + 0.25)) / 2) |> ungroup()
ea <- ggplot(e_tmp, aes(fill = temp)) + geom_rect(aes(xmin = hour, xmax = hour + 3600, ymin = top, ymax = bot)) +
  scale_y_reverse() + scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "inferno", name = "°C") + e_v + e_x + labs(x = NULL, y = "Depth (m)", tag = "a")
eb <- ggplot(eh, aes(hour, d_rho)) + e_band + geom_hline(yintercept = strat_drho_threshold(), linetype = 3) + geom_line(linewidth = 0.3) + e_v + e_x +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Δρ (kg/m³)", tag = "b")
ec <- eh |> select(hour, `1 m` = do_1, `20 m` = do_20) |> pivot_longer(-hour) |>
  ggplot(aes(hour, value, colour = name)) + e_band + geom_line(linewidth = 0.3) + e_v + e_x +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`1 m` = "#41AB5D", `20 m` = "purple4")) + labs(x = NULL, y = "DO (mg/L)", colour = NULL, tag = "c")
ed <- ggplot(eh, aes(hour, wind)) + e_band + geom_line(linewidth = 0.25, colour = "grey45") +
  geom_line(data = e_day, aes(day, wind), colour = "black", linewidth = 0.6) + e_v + e_x + labs(x = NULL, y = "Wind (m/s)", tag = "d")
ee <- ggplot(eh, aes(hour, q_net)) + e_band + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey50") + geom_line(linewidth = 0.2, colour = "grey55") +
  geom_line(data = e_day, aes(day, q_net), colour = "black", linewidth = 0.6) + e_v + e_x + labs(x = NULL, y = "Heat flux (W/m²)", tag = "e")
(ea / eb / ec / ed / ee) + plot_layout(heights = c(1.4, 0.8, 0.8, 0.8, 0.8), guides = "collect")
```

```{r}
#| label: s1415-numbers
e_in <- eh |> filter(hour >= as.POSIXct("2014-12-19", tz = "Etc/GMT-12"), hour < as.POSIXct("2015-02-09", tz = "Etc/GMT-12"))
e_lt1 <- sum(!is_stratified(e_in$d_rho), na.rm = TRUE)
e_dc <- e_in |> mutate(hr = as.integer(format(hour, "%H"))) |> group_by(hr) |>
  summarise(t_s = mean(t_s, na.rm = TRUE), wind = mean(wind, na.rm = TRUE), q = mean(q_net, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
e_56 <- eh |> filter(hour >= as.POSIXct("2015-02-05", tz = "Etc/GMT-12"), hour < as.POSIXct("2015-02-07", tz = "Etc/GMT-12"))
```

**What the hourly record adds.**

- **The stratification was continuous.** The density difference was at or below the threshold in only `r e_lt1` of `r nrow(e_in)` hours. All of these were at the onset (19 December) and the breakdown (6–8 February). There was no hidden mixing in between, and the bottom water stayed anoxic from mid-January (@fig-strat-1415).
- **The daily cycle is large, but did not break the stratification.**
  - The surface warmed by about `r sprintf("%.1f", diff(range(e_dc$t_s)))` °C from dawn to mid-afternoon.
  - The wind followed a sea-breeze-like cycle, from about `r sprintf("%.1f", min(e_dc$wind))` m/s in the morning to `r sprintf("%.1f", max(e_dc$wind))` m/s in the late afternoon. The windiest hours came while the surface was still warm and stable.
  - Every night the lake lost about 200 W/m² (hourly fluxes reached −400 to −500 W/m² on cool, windy nights). That cooling deepened the surface layer but did not reach the bottom.
- **Onset.** A windy, wet 17 December (14 hours above 8 m/s) mixed the lake. Two calm days followed, gaining 140–170 W/m², and the lake stratified on 19 December.
- **The stratification was eroded from above for a week first.** From about 30 January the warm surface layer deepened from about 10 m to about 15 m, and the surface–bottom temperature difference fell steadily from about 4.5 to 2 °C, under modest wind and a near-zero daily heat balance. By the time the storm arrived, only the bottom few metres were still isolated.
- **The breakdown came on 6 February, earlier than the daily record first showed.**
  - A windy spell built from 3 February. Then, on 5–6 February, the wind was above 8 m/s for `r sum(e_56$wind > 8, na.rm = TRUE)` of 48 hours (peak `r sprintf("%.1f", max(e_56$wind, na.rm = TRUE))` m/s), the air cooled to 14 °C and the lake lost about 140–260 W/m² a day.
  - Bottom DO jumped from 0 to 8 mg/L during 6 February, when the lake fully mixed.
  - In the daily-mean record, 6 February still just counts as stratified (density difference 0.21 kg/m³), 7 February is mixed, and the lake re-stratified weakly on 8 February. With the 2-day gap rule, the period therefore "ended" on 8 February. The forcing window then missed the storm, and this breakdown was first classed as having no unusual weather.
- **What changed as a result.** Breakdowns are now dated by the first mixed day in the last days of a period, ignoring the bridged gap. This moved `r sum(sd_br$day0 < sd_br$end + 1)` of the `r nrow(sd_br)` breakdowns earlier. The 2014/15 breakdown is now dated 7 February, one day after the hourly record, and classed as wind + cooling.
  - The "no unusual weather" class shrank only slightly, so most of it is not this artefact.
  - Some breakdowns are probably still mistimed by a day or so. Classifying them on sub-daily data (daily minimum surface–bottom difference, the hourly wind maximum and night-time cooling) for the whole record is the next refinement.

**Caveats.**

- **Wind.** Buoy wind at 10 m (converted from about 1.5–2 m when it was loaded). Lake numbers scale with the wind, but the percentiles and the classes do not.
- **Heat budget.** Uses ERA5-BC radiation and daily means, and is about 17 W/m² short of closing (see above). Only departures and percentiles are interpreted.
- **Censored and excluded periods.** Stratified periods that end in a data gap (such as 2021/22) are excluded from the breakdown statistics.
- **Definition of "stratified".** Since November 2026, a bottom − surface density difference of more than 0.2 kg/m³ (`strat_drho_threshold()` in `R/wq_synthesis_helpers.R`, used for every buoy, CTD and model metric on this page and in the calibration targets). It replaced a 1 °C temperature difference, which is a different stability at different temperatures: 0.09 kg/m³ at 10 °C, but 0.24 kg/m³ at 23 °C.
  - 0.2 kg/m³ equals 1 °C at about 20–21 °C, so summer results barely changed: 97% of buoy days are classed the same, and the longest periods are unchanged.
  - The change removed short, weak spring "stratification", which a 1 °C rule counted in cool water. The share of September days stratified fell from 9% to 2%, and the number of buoy-recorded stratified periods from 94 to 86.
  - A lower threshold (0.1 kg/m³) would add about 600 weakly stratified summer days, many of them only afternoon surface warming.
- **Not tested.** Rain and inflows (cold, dense storm water) and wind direction (fetch) are not yet tested. Several breakdowns, such as February 2022, coincide with large storms.

### Seasonal cycle of bottom-water nutrients

```{r}
#| label: fig-int-load-season
#| fig-cap: "Top: NH4-N, DRP and TP in the bottom (BOT) and integrated (INT) samples, for the pre-alum period, the first decade of dosing and the last decade. Lines are the median over years of each month's value (mean of Sites 2 and 5), and the bands the 25th–75th percentiles over years: a wide band means the median rests on a few unusual years. Numbers along the top are the years with a bottom sample in each month. Bottom: the bottom − integrated difference (the excess that internal loading builds up below the thermocline) for every hydrological year and month; blank tiles have no paired samples, and the dashed lines separate the three periods."
#| fig-height: 11
era_cut <- function(date) cut(date, as.Date(c("1980-01-01", "2006-07-01", "2016-07-01", "2030-01-01")),
                              labels = c("1990–2006 (pre-alum)", "2006–2016", "2016–2026"))
mon_lev <- month.abb[c(7:12, 1:6)]
lm_ <- lw |>
  filter(variable %in% c("nh4", "drp", "tp")) |>
  mutate(era = era_cut(date), hy = wq_hy(date),
         month = factor(month.abb[as.integer(format(date, "%m"))], mon_lev),
         variable = factor(var_lab[variable], var_lab[c("nh4", "drp", "tp")]))
# one value per hydrological year and month (mean of the two sites); median and IQR over years
lm_y <- lm_ |>
  filter(layer %in% c("BOT", "INT")) |>
  group_by(era, layer, variable, hy, month) |>
  summarise(value = mean(value), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(layer = factor(layer, c("INT", "BOT")))
lm_q <- lm_y |> group_by(era, layer, variable, month) |>
  summarise(med = median(value), q25 = quantile(value, .25), q75 = quantile(value, .75), n_yr = n(), .groups = "drop")
p_a <- ggplot(lm_q, aes(month, med, colour = layer, fill = layer, group = layer)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = q25, ymax = q75), alpha = 0.2, colour = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) + geom_point(size = 0.9) +
  geom_text(data = filter(lm_q, layer == "BOT"), aes(y = Inf, label = n_yr), vjust = 1.3, size = 2.2,
            colour = "grey30", show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_grid(variable ~ era, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.14))) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal_layer[c("INT", "BOT")], aesthetics = c("colour", "fill")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "mg/m³ (median and IQR over years)", colour = "Layer", fill = "Layer") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, size = 7))
# bottom - integrated excess per year and month
exc_y <- lm_ |>
  filter(layer %in% c("BOT", "INT")) |>
  group_by(site, date, hy, month, variable, layer) |>
  summarise(value = mean(value), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = layer, values_from = value) |>
  filter(is.finite(BOT), is.finite(INT)) |>
  group_by(hy, month, variable) |>
  summarise(excess = mean(BOT - INT), .groups = "drop")
exc_cap <- c(300, 40, 60)   # colour scale caps (NH4, DRP, TP); larger values shown at the cap
heat_one <- function(k) {
  v <- levels(exc_y$variable)[k]
  ggplot(filter(exc_y, variable == v), aes(month, hy, fill = excess)) +
    geom_tile() +
    geom_hline(yintercept = c(2006.5, 2016.5), linetype = 2, colour = "grey30", linewidth = 0.3) +
    scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166AC", mid = "white", high = "#B2182B", midpoint = 0,
                         limits = c(-exc_cap[k] / 3, exc_cap[k]), oob = scales::squish, name = NULL) +
    scale_y_reverse(breaks = seq(1990, 2026, 4), expand = c(0, 0)) +
    scale_x_discrete(drop = FALSE) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = if (k == 1) "Hydrological year" else NULL, title = paste("BOT − INT:", v)) +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, size = 7), plot.title = element_text(size = 9),
          legend.position = "bottom", legend.key.width = unit(1, "cm"), legend.key.height = unit(0.25, "cm"),
          panel.grid = element_blank())
}
p_b <- heat_one(1) | heat_one(2) | heat_one(3)
p_a / p_b + plot_layout(heights = c(1.6, 1.4))
```

**The internal-loading signal follows stratification closely.**
